How to prepare a drinkware RFQ that returns a firm price

The most useful first enquiry makes the finished product visible: model, capacity, quantity split, logo, packaging, destination and date. Here is the checklist we work from — and a plain-text template you can copy.

A good RFQ is short, but it makes the product visible

The hardest enquiries to answer are not the short ones — they are the ones that leave out the quantity per size, the accessories in one selling unit, or the destination. When those details are missing, the supplier fills the gaps with assumptions, and the prices that come back look comparable but describe different products.

A good RFQ identifies the product, the capacity, the quantity and its split, the customisation, the packaging, the destination and the date. If a decision is still open, say so — an open question gets one clarifying reply; a wrong assumption gets a quotation for the wrong product.

Start from the closest model

Send a product link, a model number, a drawing or a reference photo. A model number is best because it connects your enquiry to a real body — the capacity, the material and the case pack already exist on the record.

If your reference comes from another source, say which features must match and which can change. Do not assume a photograph carries dimensions: perspective distorts proportions, and most product images never show the usable capacity.

State the use and the sales channel

A tasting-room merchandise glass, a six-piece retail set, a banquet tumbler and an e-commerce gift item need different accessories, decoration and packing. The channel also decides which use statements matter. We do not infer washing, microwave or thermal performance from appearance — if your market needs a specific claim, name it so it can be reviewed against the selected product and the evidence on file.

Give the capacity and the dimensions that must fit

Capacity affects the body, the pack size and the freight volume. Write the target in millilitres or ounces and say whether it is fixed. If a dimension matters — a refrigerator door, a shelf height, an existing lid — include it, and for sets list the capacity of every component. When several sizes are involved, list the quantity for each: a capacity range is not one product.

Show the total quantity and the complete split

A total on its own is not enough once the order contains several colours, capacities or logos. Write the total, then break it down — quantity per size, per colour, per logo version, and how the pieces pack into sets. The same total divided differently is a different production plan, and it is the split, not the headline, that sets the workable minimum.

Define the logo and the visible customisation

Attach a vector file if you have one, and state the colour, the approximate size, the position and the process if you know it. If you do not know the process, describe the appearance and the use condition and we will propose one. For colour projects, give a controlled reference such as a Pantone number and the quantity per colour.

Treat the product artwork and the packaging artwork as two separate files and two separate approvals. A clear artwork file reduces sampling errors, and the approved decorated sample is what controls bulk production.

List every component in one selling unit

A lid, a sleeve, a stopper, a base or an insert changes the product. Write the exact quantity of each component per unit or per set, and list replacement components separately. A quotation should state what is included, so you are never comparing a bare-product price against a complete-item price.

Describe the packaging and the sales unit

Tell us how you will receive and sell the product:

  • Bulk divided export carton
  • Individual plain or custom colour box
  • Pair or multi-piece retail set
  • Gift box with insert
  • E-commerce pack for single-unit delivery
  • Hospitality pack with practical dividers

State the pieces per set and any barcode, label, country-mark or carton-mark requirement. Packaging is developed around the approved product and its accessories; it affects the finished unit cost, the carton dimensions, the freight volume and the schedule. A retail box does not automatically survive last-mile parcel delivery.

Add the destination, the trade basis and the date that matters

At minimum we need the destination country or warehouse city. State the trade basis you use — FOB, EXW, DDP — or say you are unsure and we will propose a route. Freight-related prices are time-sensitive, so the destination and the quotation date matter.

Give the date the goods are needed and say what it is: a shipment date, a warehouse arrival date and a retail launch date are three different milestones, and we plan backwards from the right one. For seasonal projects, put the non-negotiable launch date in the first message — late packaging artwork is the most common way a simple order loses time.

Say what the sample must prove

A plain sample checks size and hand feel. A decorated sample approves the logo. A complete set checks component fit. A packaging sample approves the box and the insert. Say which one you need, and record the approved version — model, capacity, decoration file, accessories and pack — so production instructions never rely on scattered messages.

Send this in an email or through the quote form on this site. You do not need to complete every line before contacting us — mark open decisions as open.

Questions on this topic

What is the minimum information you need for a firm quotation?

The closest model or reference, the capacity, the total quantity with its split per size, colour and logo version, the packaging requirement, the destination and the target date. Those details let us price the finished item rather than a bare product.

Open the quote form

Can I request a quote from a photo alone?

Yes, as a starting point. Add the target capacity, the expected quantity, the use, the packaging and the destination, and we will compare the photo with current models and name the missing specifications before pricing.

Do I need finished artwork before asking for a price?

No. State the box type, the pieces per set, the channel and the destination. Artwork can follow — but the packaging scope has to be in the estimate, because it affects both cost and schedule.

Should I ask for FOB or DDP pricing?

State the trade basis you normally use. If you are unsure, give the destination and we will propose the available routes. Freight-related prices change over time, so they are always tied to a date.

What file format should the logo be?

A vector file is preferred when available. Also state the logo colour, the approximate size and the position. The approved decorated sample — not the file alone — is what controls bulk production.

How quickly can I get a sample?

It depends on stock status. In-stock samples are dispatched within 1–3 working days after payment is received; for no-stock small batches, including samples, FOB dispatch normally takes 10–15 days. These are dispatch times, not arrival times — destination freight is quoted separately.

Why do you ask for the quantity per colour?

Because the split, not the total, sets the production plan. Quantity per colour and per logo version decides how many production groups the order contains, which drives setup, counting, packing and cost.

What if I cannot answer every field?

Mark it as open and send the enquiry anyway. An open question gets one clarifying reply; a wrong assumption gets a quotation for the wrong product, and that costs both sides more time.
